This Neapolis was built to the east, and substantial walls were erected around the entire settlement for protection against external threats. Sections of these fortifications remain visible in the Cassaro district. The district itself takes its name from the walls, with "Cassaro" originating from the Arabic word *al-qsr* (castle or stronghold). The walls featured limited access points, indicating that trade with the island's interior was common. Additionally, some research suggests there may also have been walls separating the old city from the new one. The colony was organized around a central street, or decumanus, intersected perpendicularly by smaller streets. This main thoroughfare is known today as the Corso Vittorio Emanuele.

input: During the 16th and 17th centuries slave traders began to raid the region as part of the expansion of the Saharan and Nile River slave routes. Their captives were slaved and shipped to the Mediterranean coast, Europe, Arabia, the Western Hemisphere, or to the slave ports and factories along the West and North Africa or South the Ubanqui and Congo rivers. In the mid 19th century, the Bobangi people became major slave traders and sold their captives to the Americas using the Ubangi river to reach the coast. During the 18th century Bandia-Nzakara peoples established the Bangassou Kingdom along the Ubangi River.

input: Early Islamic philosophy and Islamic metaphysics, imbued as it is with Islamic theology, distinguishes more clearly than Aristotelianism between essence and existence. Whereas existence is the domain of the contingent and the accidental, essence endures within a being beyond the accidental. The philosophy of Ibn Sīnā, particularly that part relating to metaphysics, owes much to al-Farabi. The search for a definitive Islamic philosophy separate from Occasionalism can be seen in what is left of his work.
rewrite: Early Islamic philosophy and metaphysics, deeply infused with Islamic theology, draws a sharper distinction between essence and existence than Aristotelianism does. Existence belongs to the realm of the contingent and accidental, while essence persists in a being beyond such accidents. Ibn Sīnā’s metaphysical philosophy is greatly indebted to al-Farabi. The pursuit of a distinct Islamic philosophy apart from Occasionalism is evident in the surviving portions of his work.

input: The majority of British Jews live in London, with significant Jewish communities in Stamford Hill, Stanmore, Golders Green, Finchley, Hampstead, Hendon and Edgware in North London. Bevis Marks Synagogue in the City of London is affiliated to London's historic Sephardic Jewish community. It is the only synagogue in Europe which has held regular services continuously for over 300 years. Stanmore and Canons Park Synagogue has the largest membership of any single Orthodox synagogue in the whole of Europe, overtaking Ilford synagogue (also in London) in 1998. The community set up the London Jewish Forum in 2006 in response to the growing significance of devolved London Government.

The Bevis Marks Synagogue in the City of London is part of the historic Sephardic community and is unique in Europe for holding regular services continuously for more than 300 years. Meanwhile, the Stanmore and Canons Park Synagogue has the largest membership of any Orthodox synagogue in Europe, having surpassed Ilford synagogue (also in London) in 1998. In response to the increasing importance of devolved London Government, the community established the London Jewish Forum in 2006.

input: So that the maximum number of colors can be accurately reproduced on your computer screen, each color has been given a code number, or sRGB, which tells your computer the intensity of the red, green and blue components of that color. The intensity of each component is measured on a scale of zero to 255, which means the complete list includes 16,777,216 distinct colors and shades. The sRGB number of pure red, for example, is 255, 00, 00, which means the red component is at its maximum intensity, and there is no green or blue. The sRGB number for crimson is 220, 20, 60, which means that the red is slightly less intense and therefore darker, there is some green, which leans it toward orange; and there is a larger amount of blue,which makes it slightly blue-violet.

Each component is measured on a scale from 0 to 255, resulting in a total of 16,777,216 distinct colors and shades. For instance, pure red has an sRGB value of 255, 00, 00, indicating maximum red intensity with no green or blue. Crimson is coded as 220, 20, 60, where the red is slightly less intense and therefore darker, a small amount of green shifts it toward orange, and a larger amount of blue gives it a slightly blue-violet tone.

input: New Haven was the location of one of Jim Morrison's infamous arrests while he fronted the rock group The Doors. The near-riotous concert and arrest in 1967 at the New Haven Arena was commemorated by Morrison in the lyrics to "Peace Frog" which include the line "...blood in the streets in the town of New Haven..." This was the first time a rock star had ever been arrested in concert.[citation needed] This event is portrayed in the movie The Doors (1991), starring Val Kilmer as Morrison, with a concert hall in Los Angeles used to depict the New Haven Arena.

This marked the first time a rock star had ever been arrested during a concert.[citation needed] The event is portrayed in the 1991 film *The Doors*, starring Val Kilmer as Morrison, with a concert hall in Los Angeles standing in for the New Haven Arena.

input: When Zeus struck down Apollo's son Asclepius with a lightning bolt for resurrecting Hippolytus from the dead (transgressing Themis by stealing Hades's subjects), Apollo in revenge killed the Cyclopes, who had fashioned the bolt for Zeus. Apollo would have been banished to Tartarus forever for this, but was instead sentenced to one year of hard labor, due to the intercession of his mother, Leto. During this time he served as shepherd for King Admetus of Pherae in Thessaly. Admetus treated Apollo well, and, in return, the god conferred great benefits on Admetus.

input: Symptoms of mild zinc deficiency are diverse. Clinical outcomes include depressed growth, diarrhea, impotence and delayed sexual maturation, alopecia, eye and skin lesions, impaired appetite, altered cognition, impaired host defense properties, defects in carbohydrate utilization, and reproductive teratogenesis. Mild zinc deficiency depresses immunity, although excessive zinc does also. Animals with a diet deficient in zinc require twice as much food in order to attain the same weight gain as animals given sufficient zinc.

input: Although not a centre for handicrafts itself, the patronage of the arts by the Mughals and Nizams attracted artisans from the region to Hyderabad. Such crafts include: Bidriware, a metalwork handicraft from neighbouring Karnataka, which was popularised during the 18th century and has since been granted a Geographical Indication (GI) tag under the auspices of the WTO act; and Zari and Zardozi, embroidery works on textile that involve making elaborate designs using gold, silver and other metal threads. Another example of a handicraft drawn to Hyderabad is Kalamkari, a hand-painted or block-printed cotton textile that comes from cities in Andhra Pradesh. This craft is distinguished in having both a Hindu style, known as Srikalahasti and entirely done by hand, and an Islamic style, known as Machilipatnam that uses both hand and block techniques. Examples of Hyderabad's arts and crafts are housed in various museums including the Salar Jung Museum (housing "one of the largest one-man-collections in the world"), the AP State Archaeology Museum, the Nizam Museum, the City Museum and the Birla Science Museum.

Among these crafts is Bidriware, a metalwork tradition originating in neighboring Karnataka. Popularized in the 18th century, it now holds a Geographical Indication (GI) tag under the WTO act. Also prominent are Zari and Zardozi, forms of embroidery that create elaborate designs using gold, silver, and other metal threads on textiles. It features two distinct styles: the Hindu Srikalahasti style, executed entirely by hand, and the Islamic Machilipatnam style, which employs both hand-painting and block-printing. Examples of these and other local arts and crafts are displayed in several museums, such as the Salar Jung Museum (noted for "one of the largest one-man-collections in the world"), the AP State Archaeology Museum, the Nizam Museum, the City Museum, and the Birla Science Museum.

input: Midway through the 19th century, the focus of geology shifted from description and classification to attempts to understand how the surface of the Earth had changed. The first comprehensive theories of mountain building were proposed during this period, as were the first modern theories of earthquakes and volcanoes. Louis Agassiz and others established the reality of continent-covering ice ages, and "fluvialists" like Andrew Crombie Ramsay argued that river valleys were formed, over millions of years by the rivers that flow through them. After the discovery of radioactivity, radiometric dating methods were developed, starting in the 20th century. Alfred Wegener's theory of "continental drift" was widely dismissed when he proposed it in the 1910s, but new data gathered in the 1950s and 1960s led to the theory of plate tectonics, which provided a plausible mechanism for it. Plate tectonics also provided a unified explanation for a wide range of seemingly unrelated geological phenomena. Since 1970 it has served as the unifying principle in geology.
rewrite: During the mid-19th century, geology’s emphasis moved beyond mere description and classification toward understanding the processes that shaped the Earth’s surface. This era saw the proposal of the first comprehensive theories of mountain building, alongside the first modern explanations for earthquakes and volcanoes. Louis Agassiz and others confirmed the existence of continent-spanning ice ages, while "fluvialists" such as Andrew Crombie Ramsay contended that river valleys were carved over millions of years by the rivers within them. Following the discovery of radioactivity, radiometric dating techniques emerged in the 20th century. Alfred Wegener’s theory of "continental drift," introduced in the 1910s, was largely rejected initially. However, new evidence collected in the 1950s and 1960s led to the theory of plate tectonics, which supplied a convincing mechanism for continental movement. Plate tectonics also offered a unified account for many seemingly disconnected geological phenomena. Since 1970, it has stood as the unifying principle in geology.

input: The patron saint of Galicia is Saint James the Greater, whose body was discovered – according to the Catholic tradition – in 814 near Compostela. After that date, the relics of Saint James became an extraordinary centre of pilgrimage and from the 9th century have been kept in the heart of the church – the modern-day cathedral – dedicated to him. There are many other Galician and associated saints; some of the best-known are: Saint Ansurius, Saint Rudesind, Saint Mariña of Augas Santas, Saint Senorina, Trahamunda and Froilan.

input: After World War II Hudson's realized that the limited parking space at its downtown skyscraper would increasingly be a problem for its customers. The solution in 1954 was to open the Northland Center in nearby Southfield, just beyond the city limits. It was the largest suburban shopping center in the world, and quickly became the main shopping destination for northern and western Detroit, and for much of the suburbs. By 1961 the downtown skyscraper accounted for only half of Hudson's sales; it closed in 1986. The Northland Center Hudson's, rebranded Macy's in 2006 following acquisition by Federated Department Stores, was closed along with the remaining stores in the center in March 2015 due to the mall's high storefront vacancy, decaying infrastructure, and financial mismanagement.

In 1712 there were 318 men employed and by 1733 it had grown to a population of 3,000 people.

input: Ibn Sina's first appointment was that of physician to the emir, Nuh II, who owed him his recovery from a dangerous illness (997). Ibn Sina's chief reward for this service was access to the royal library of the Samanids, well-known patrons of scholarship and scholars. When the library was destroyed by fire not long after, the enemies of Ibn Sina accused him of burning it, in order for ever to conceal the sources of his knowledge. Meanwhile, he assisted his father in his financial labors, but still found time to write some of his earliest works.

input: With a population of 518,000, Hanover is a major centre of Northern Germany and the country's thirteenth largest city. Hanover also hosts annual commercial trade fairs such as the Hanover Fair and the CeBIT. Every year Hanover hosts the Schützenfest Hannover, the world's largest marksmen's festival, and the Oktoberfest Hannover, the second largest Oktoberfest in the world (beside Oktoberfest of Blumenau). In 2000, Hanover hosted the world fair Expo 2000. The Hanover fairground, due to numerous extensions, especially for the Expo 2000, is the largest in the world. Hanover is of national importance because of its universities and medical school, its international airport and its large zoo. The city is also a major crossing point of railway lines and highways (Autobahnen), connecting European main lines in both the east-west (Berlin–Ruhr area) and north-south (Hamburg–Munich, etc.) directions.

The city is also home to the Schützenfest Hannover, the world's largest marksmen's festival, and the Oktoberfest Hannover, the second largest Oktoberfest globally. In 2000, Hanover hosted the world fair Expo 2000. The Hanover fairground, expanded notably for that event, is the largest in the world. The city holds national importance due to its universities and medical school, its international airport, and its large zoo. Furthermore, Hanover is a major junction for railway lines and highways (Autobahnen), connecting key European routes in both east-west and north-south directions.

input: Although the Reformation was a religious movement, it also had a strong impact on all other aspects of life: marriage and family, education, the humanities and sciences, the political and social order, the economy, and the arts. Protestant churches reject the idea of a celibate priesthood and thus allow their clergy to marry. Many of their families contributed to the development of intellectual elites in their countries. Since about 1950, women have entered the ministry, and some have assumed leading positions (e.g. bishops), in most Protestant churches.
rewrite: While the Reformation was fundamentally a religious movement, its influence extended deeply into all areas of life, including marriage, family, education, the humanities, sciences, political and social order, economy, and the arts. Protestant churches, rejecting a celibate priesthood, permit clergy to marry. Their families often helped form intellectual elites in their nations. Since around 1950, most Protestant churches have also admitted women into the ministry, with some attaining leadership roles such as bishop.

input: At Princeton, the physicist Robert R. Wilson encouraged Feynman to participate in the Manhattan Project—the wartime U.S. Army project at Los Alamos developing the atomic bomb. Feynman said he was persuaded to join this effort to build it before Nazi Germany developed their own bomb. He was assigned to Hans Bethe's theoretical division and impressed Bethe enough to be made a group leader. He and Bethe developed the Bethe–Feynman formula for calculating the yield of a fission bomb, which built upon previous work by Robert Serber.
rewrite: At Princeton, physicist Robert R. Wilson encouraged Richard Feynman to join the Manhattan Project, the U.S. Army's wartime effort in Los Alamos to develop the atomic bomb. Feynman stated he was convinced to participate in order to help build the weapon before Nazi Germany could create its own. Assigned to Hans Bethe's theoretical division, Feynman impressed Bethe and was promoted to group leader. Together, they derived the Bethe–Feynman formula for calculating fission bomb yield, expanding on earlier work by Robert Serber.

input: London is the seat of the Government of the United Kingdom. Many government departments are based close to the Palace of Westminster, particularly along Whitehall, including the Prime Minister's residence at 10 Downing Street. The British Parliament is often referred to as the "Mother of Parliaments" (although this sobriquet was first applied to England itself by John Bright) because it has been the model for most other parliamentary systems. There are 73 Members of Parliament (MPs) from London, who correspond to local parliamentary constituencies in the national Parliament. As of May 2015, 45 are from the Labour Party, 27 are Conservatives, and one is a Liberal Democrat.
rewrite: London serves as the seat of the United Kingdom’s Government. Numerous government departments are located near the Palace of Westminster, especially along Whitehall; this includes the Prime Minister’s residence at 10 Downing Street. The British Parliament is frequently called the "Mother of Parliaments"—a term first applied to England by John Bright—as it has been the model for many other parliamentary systems. London is represented by 73 Members of Parliament (MPs), corresponding to local constituencies in the national Parliament. As of May 2015, these comprised 45 Labour Party members, 27 Conservatives, and one Liberal Democrat.

input: In 1681, in partial repayment of a debt, Charles II of England granted William Penn a charter for what would become the Pennsylvania colony. Despite the royal charter, Penn bought the land from the local Lenape to be on good terms with the Native Americans and ensure peace for his colony. Penn made a treaty of friendship with Lenape chief Tammany under an elm tree at Shackamaxon, in what is now the city's Fishtown section. Penn named the city Philadelphia, which is Greek for brotherly love (from philos, "love" or "friendship", and adelphos, "brother"). As a Quaker, Penn had experienced religious persecution and wanted his colony to be a place where anyone could worship freely. This tolerance, far more than afforded by most other colonies, led to better relations with the local Native tribes and fostered Philadelphia's rapid growth into America's most important city. Penn planned a city on the Delaware River to serve as a port and place for government. Hoping that Philadelphia would become more like an English rural town instead of a city, Penn laid out roads on a grid plan to keep houses and businesses spread far apart, with areas for gardens and orchards. The city's inhabitants did not follow Penn's plans, as they crowded by the Delaware River, the port, and subdivided and resold their lots. Before Penn left Philadelphia for the last time, he issued the Charter of 1701 establishing it as a city. It became an important trading center, poor at first, but with tolerable living conditions by the 1750s. Benjamin Franklin, a leading citizen, helped improve city services and founded new ones, such as fire protection, a library, and one of the American colonies' first hospitals.
rewrite:
In 1681, Charles II of England granted William Penn a charter for the Pennsylvania colony, partially repaying a debt. Although he held this royal charter, Penn also purchased the land from the local Lenape people to establish good relations and ensure peace for his new colony. He famously made a treaty of friendship with Lenape chief Tammany under an elm tree at Shackamaxon, located in what is now the Fishtown section of the city. Penn named the city Philadelphia, derived from the Greek words for brotherly love (from *philos*, meaning "love" or "friendship," and *adelphos*, meaning "brother"). A Quaker who had experienced religious persecution, Penn intended his colony to be a place of free worship for all. This unusual degree of tolerance, far greater than in most other colonies, contributed to better relations with local Native tribes and supported Philadelphia's rapid growth into America's most important city.

Penn planned the city along the Delaware River to function as both a port and a seat of government. Hoping Philadelphia would resemble a spacious English rural town rather than a dense city, he designed a grid plan with roads, keeping houses and businesses widely spaced and including areas for gardens and orchards. However, the inhabitants did not follow this plan, instead crowding near the Delaware River and the port, and subdividing and reselling their lots. Before Penn left Philadelphia for the final time, he issued the Charter of 1701, which formally established it as a city. It grew into a vital trading center, initially poor but with living conditions that had become tolerable by the 1750s. The leading citizen Benjamin Franklin helped enhance city services and founded new ones, including fire protection, a library, and one of the first hospitals in the American colonies.

input: On 20 April 1992, The Freddie Mercury Tribute Concert was held at London's Wembley Stadium to a 72,000-strong crowd. Performers, including Def Leppard, Robert Plant, Guns N' Roses, Elton John, David Bowie, George Michael, Annie Lennox, Seal, Extreme, and Metallica performed various Queen songs along with the three remaining Queen members (and Spike Edney.) The concert is listed in the Guinness Book of Records as "The largest rock star benefit concert", as it was televised to over 1.2 billion viewers worldwide, and raised over £20,000,000 for AIDS charities.

input: Daylighting is the oldest method of interior lighting. Daylighting is simply designing a space to use as much natural light as possible. This decreases energy consumption and costs, and requires less heating and cooling from the building. Daylighting has also been proven to have positive effects on patients in hospitals as well as work and school performance. Due to a lack of information that indicate the likely energy savings, daylighting schemes are not yet popular among most buildings.
rewrite: Daylighting, the oldest method of interior lighting, involves designing spaces to maximize natural light. This reduces energy consumption and costs while decreasing the need for building heating and cooling. It has also been shown to benefit hospital patients and improve performance in workplaces and schools. However, because information indicating likely energy savings is lacking, daylighting schemes remain unpopular in most buildings.

input: After 12 years as commissioner of the AFL, David Baker retired unexpectedly on July 25, 2008, just two days before ArenaBowl XXII; deputy commissioner Ed Policy was named interim commissioner until Baker's replacement was found. Baker explained, "When I took over as commissioner, I thought it would be for one year. It turned into 12. But now it's time."

But now it's time."

input: The uneasy alliance of Carranza, Obregón, Villa, and Zapata eventually led the rebels to victory. The fight against Huerta formally ended on August 15, 1914, when Álvaro Obregón signed a number of treaties in Teoloyucan in which the last of Huerta's forces surrendered to him and recognized the constitutional government. On August 20, 1914, Carranza made a triumphal entry into Mexico City. Carranza (supported by Obregón) was now the strongest candidate to fill the power vacuum and set himself up as head of the new government. This government successfully printed money, passed laws, etc.

input: The low mechanical complexity of hydraulic elevators in comparison to traction elevators makes them ideal for low rise, low traffic installations. They are less energy efficient as the pump works against gravity to push the car and its passengers upwards; this energy is lost when the car descends on its own weight. The high current draw of the pump when starting up also places higher demands on a building’s electrical system. There are also environmental concerns should the lifting cylinder leak fluid into the ground.
rewrite: Hydraulic elevators have low mechanical complexity compared to traction elevators, making them suitable for low-rise, low-traffic installations. However, they are less energy efficient because the pump works against gravity to lift the car; this energy is lost when the car descends by its own weight. The pump's high starting current also places greater demands on a building's electrical system. Additionally, environmental concerns arise if the lifting cylinder leaks fluid into the ground.

input: Muslim rule started in parts of north India in the 13th century when the Delhi Sultanate was founded in 1206 CE by the Central Asian Turks. The Delhi Sultanate ruled the major part of northern India in the early 14th century, but declined in the late 14th century when several powerful Hindu states such as the Vijayanagara Empire, Gajapati Kingdom, Ahom Kingdom, as well as Rajput dynasties and states, such as Mewar dynasty, emerged. The 15th century saw the emergence of Sikhism. In the 16th century, Mughals came from Central Asia and gradually covered most of India. The Mughal Empire suffered a gradual decline in the early 18th century, which provided opportunities for the Maratha Empire, Sikh Empire and Mysore Kingdom to exercise control over large areas of the subcontinent.
rewrite: Muslim rule in north India began in the 13th century with the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate in 1206 CE by Central Asian Turks. The Sultanate dominated much of northern India in the early 14th century but waned in the late 14th century. This decline coincided with the rise of several powerful Hindu states, including the Vijayanagara Empire, the Gajapati Kingdom, the Ahom Kingdom, and Rajput dynasties like Mewar. The 15th century witnessed the emergence of Sikhism. During the 16th century, the Mughals arrived from Central Asia and eventually came to rule most of India. Their empire entered a gradual decline in the early 18th century, creating opportunities for the Maratha Empire, the Sikh Empire, and the Mysore Kingdom to exert control over vast regions of the subcontinent.

input: John, the youngest of five sons of King Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine, was at first not expected to inherit significant lands. Following the failed rebellion of his elder brothers between 1173 and 1174, however, John became Henry's favourite child. He was appointed the Lord of Ireland in 1177 and given lands in England and on the continent. John's elder brothers William, Henry and Geoffrey died young; by the time Richard I became king in 1189, John was a potential heir to the throne. John unsuccessfully attempted a rebellion against Richard's royal administrators whilst his brother was participating in the Third Crusade. Despite this, after Richard died in 1199, John was proclaimed King of England, and came to an agreement with Philip II of France to recognise John's possession of the continental Angevin lands at the peace treaty of Le Goulet in 1200.
rewrite: As the youngest of King Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine's five sons, John was initially not expected to inherit substantial territory. This changed after the unsuccessful rebellion of his elder brothers from 1173 to 1174, after which John became his father's favourite. He was made Lord of Ireland in 1177 and granted lands in England and on the continent. The early deaths of his brothers William, Henry, and Geoffrey left John as a potential heir to the throne by the time Richard I became king in 1189. During Richard's involvement in the Third Crusade, John attempted a failed rebellion against the king's administrators. Nevertheless, following Richard's death in 1199, John was proclaimed King of England. He subsequently reached an agreement with Philip II of France, who recognized John's hold on the continental Angevin lands in the Peace of Le Goulet in 1200.

input: With the fall of the Western Roman Empire, there arose a more diffuse arena for political studies. The rise of monotheism and, particularly for the Western tradition, Christianity, brought to light a new space for politics and political action[citation needed]. During the Middle Ages, the study of politics was widespread in the churches and courts. Works such as Augustine of Hippo's The City of God synthesized current philosophies and political traditions with those of Christianity, redefining the borders between what was religious and what was political. Most of the political questions surrounding the relationship between Church and State were clarified and contested in this period.
rewrite: Following the fall of the Western Roman Empire, the arena for political thought became more diffuse. The ascent of monotheism, and specifically Christianity in the West, revealed a new domain for politics and political action. Throughout the Middle Ages, the study of politics was prevalent within churches and royal courts. Works like Augustine of Hippo's *The City of God* synthesized contemporary philosophy and political traditions with Christian thought, thereby redefining the boundaries between the religious and the political. It was during this era that most questions regarding the relationship between Church and State were both clarified and contested.

input: According to Thomas DeGregori, an economics professor at the University of Houston, in an article published by the Cato Institute, a libertarian think-tank operating in Washington D.C., "it is clear that technological and economic change are vital ingredients in getting children out of the workplace and into schools. Then they can grow to become productive adults and live longer, healthier lives. However, in poor countries like Bangladesh, working children are essential for survival in many families, as they were in our own heritage until the late 19th century. So, while the struggle to end child labour is necessary, getting there often requires taking different routes—and, sadly, there are many political obstacles.
rewrite: In an article for the Cato Institute, a libertarian think-tank in Washington D.C., University of Houston economics professor Thomas DeGregori states that technological and economic progress are crucial for moving children from workplaces into schools. This shift allows them to develop into productive adults with longer, healthier lives. Yet, in poor nations such as Bangladesh, child labor remains essential for family survival, much as it was in many countries until the late 19th century. Therefore, although ending child labor is a necessary goal, reaching it demands varied approaches—and is often hindered by significant political obstacles.

input: Himachal was one of the few states that had remained largely untouched by external customs, largely due to its difficult terrain. With the technological advancements the state has changed very rapidly. It is a multireligional, multicultural as well as multilingual state like other Indian states. Some of the most commonly spoken languages includes Hindi, Pahari, Dogri, Mandeali Kangri, Mandyali, Gojri and Kinnauri. The caste communities residing in Himachal include the Khatri, Brahmins of the Hindu Faith and the Sikh Brahmin Caste Bhatra, Rajputs, Gujjars, Gaddis, Ghirth (choudhary), Kannets, Rathis and Kolis, Sood There are tribal populations in the state which mainly comprise Kinnars, Pangawals, Sulehria, and Lahaulis.The people Of Himachal Pradesh are very simple and live a traditional ´Pahari' lifestyle.
rewrite: Himachal was long one of the few states largely untouched by external customs, primarily because of its difficult terrain. However, technological advancements have prompted very rapid change. Like other Indian states, it is multireligious, multicultural, and multilingual. Commonly spoken languages include Hindi, Pahari, Dogri, Mandeali, Kangri, Mandyali, Gojri, and Kinnauri. Caste communities residing there include the Khatri, Brahmins of the Hindu faith, the Sikh Brahmin caste Bhatra, Rajputs, Gujjars, Gaddis, Ghirth (choudhary), Kannets, Rathis, Kolis, and Sood. The state also has tribal populations, mainly comprising Kinnars, Pangawals, Sulehria, and Lahaulis. The people of Himachal Pradesh are known for their simplicity and traditional 'Pahari' lifestyle.

input: The term Muslim world, also known as Islamic world and the Ummah (Arabic: أمة‎, meaning "nation" or "community") has different meanings. In a religious sense, the Islamic Ummah refers to those who adhere to the teachings of Islam, referred to as Muslims. In a cultural sense, the Muslim Ummah refers to Islamic civilization, exclusive of non-Muslims living in that civilization. In a modern geopolitical sense, the term "Islamic Nation" usually refers collectively to Muslim-majority countries, states, districts, or towns.
rewrite: The term "Muslim world," also called the Islamic world or the Ummah (Arabic: أمة‎, meaning "nation" or "community"), carries various meanings. Religiously, the Islamic Ummah denotes all adherents of Islam, known as Muslims. Culturally, it refers to Islamic civilization, excluding non-Muslims within it. In a modern geopolitical sense, the term "Islamic Nation" typically refers collectively to Muslim-majority countries, states, districts, or towns.

input: The current iteration of the Canadian Armed Forces dates from 1 February 1968, when the Royal Canadian Navy, Canadian Army, and Royal Canadian Air Force were merged into a unified structure and superseded by elemental commands. Its roots, however, lie in colonial militia groups that served alongside garrisons of the French and British armies and navies; a structure that remained in place until the early 20th century. Thereafter, a distinctly Canadian army and navy was established, followed by an air force, that, because of the constitutional arrangements at the time, remained effectively under the control of the British government until Canada gained legislative independence from the United Kingdom in 1931, in part due to the distinguished achievement and sacrifice of the Canadian Corps in the First World War.
rewrite: The modern Canadian Armed Forces originated on February 1, 1968, with the unification of the Royal Canadian Navy, Canadian Army, and Royal Canadian Air Force into a single structure governed by elemental commands. Its foundations, however, are much older, tracing back to colonial militia groups that served with French and British army garrisons and naval forces—an arrangement that persisted until the early 20th century. Following that period, a distinctly Canadian army and navy were established, and later an air force. Due to the constitutional arrangements of the era, these forces remained effectively under British control until Canada achieved legislative independence from the United Kingdom in 1931. This shift was influenced in part by the distinguished service and sacrifice of the Canadian Corps during the First World War.

input: Rapid increases in a number of commodity prices followed the collapse in the housing bubble. The price of oil nearly tripled from $50 to $147 from early 2007 to 2008, before plunging as the financial crisis began to take hold in late 2008. Experts debate the causes, with some attributing it to speculative flow of money from housing and other investments into commodities, some to monetary policy, and some to the increasing feeling of raw materials scarcity in a fast-growing world, leading to long positions taken on those markets, such as Chinese increasing presence in Africa. An increase in oil prices tends to divert a larger share of consumer spending into gasoline, which creates downward pressure on economic growth in oil importing countries, as wealth flows to oil-producing states. A pattern of spiking instability in the price of oil over the decade leading up to the price high of 2008 has been recently identified. The destabilizing effects of this price variance has been proposed as a contributory factor in the financial crisis.
rewrite: Following the collapse of the housing bubble, many commodity prices rose rapidly. Notably, the price of oil surged from $50 in early 2007 to $147 by 2008, nearly tripling before it plummeted in late 2008 as the financial crisis intensified. Experts debate the causes of this spike. Some attribute it to speculative money flowing from housing and other investments into commodities, others to monetary policy, and still others to a growing perception of raw material scarcity in a fast-growing world, which led to long positions on these markets—exemplified by China's increasing presence in Africa. Higher oil prices divert a larger share of consumer spending to gasoline, creating downward pressure on economic growth in oil-importing nations as wealth transfers to oil-producing states. A pattern of spiking instability in oil prices throughout the decade preceding the 2008 peak has been recently identified. This price volatility and its destabilizing effects have been proposed as a contributory factor in the financial crisis.

input: Gaddafi was a very private individual, who described himself as a "simple revolutionary" and "pious Muslim" called upon by Allah to continue Nasser's work. Reporter Mirella Bianco found that his friends considered him particularly loyal and generous, and asserted that he adored children. She was told by Gaddafi's father that even as a child he had been "always serious, even taciturn", a trait he also exhibited in adulthood. His father said that he was courageous, intelligent, pious, and family oriented.

input: The idea of self-concept is known as the ability of a person to have opinions and beliefs that are defined confidently, consistent and stable. Early in adolescence, cognitive developments result in greater self-awareness, greater awareness of others and their thoughts and judgments, the ability to think about abstract, future possibilities, and the ability to consider multiple possibilities at once. As a result, adolescents experience a significant shift from the simple, concrete, and global self-descriptions typical of young children; as children, they defined themselves by physical traits whereas as adolescents, they define themselves based on their values, thoughts, and opinions.
rewrite: Self-concept refers to a person's ability to hold opinions and beliefs that are confidently defined, consistent, and stable. During early adolescence, cognitive development leads to increased self-awareness, a greater understanding of others and their perspectives, and the capacity for abstract and future-oriented thought, including considering multiple possibilities simultaneously. Consequently, adolescents undergo a significant shift from the simple, concrete, and global self-descriptions characteristic of young children. While children often define themselves by physical traits, adolescents tend to define themselves based on their values, thoughts, and opinions.

input: The University of Plymouth enrolls 25,895 total students as of 2014/15 (22nd largest in the UK out of 165). It also employs 3,000 staff with an annual income of around £160 million. It was founded in 1992 from Polytechnic South West (formerly Plymouth Polytechnic) following the Further and Higher Education Act 1992. It has courses in maritime business, marine engineering, marine biology and Earth, ocean and environmental sciences, surf science, shipping and logistics. The university formed a joint venture with the fellow Devonian University of Exeter in 2000, establishing the Peninsula College of Medicine and Dentistry. The college is ranked 8th out of 30 universities in the UK in 2011 for medicine. Its dental school was established in 2006, which also provides free dental care in an attempt to improve access to dental care in the South West.
rewrite: The University of Plymouth had a total enrollment of 25,895 students in the 2014/15 academic year, making it the 22nd largest institution out of 165 in the UK. It employs approximately 3,000 staff and has an annual income of around £160 million. Founded in 1992 under the Further and Higher Education Act, it originated from Polytechnic South West, which was formerly known as Plymouth Polytechnic. The university offers courses in maritime business, marine engineering, marine biology, Earth, ocean and environmental sciences, surf science, shipping, and logistics. In 2000, it formed a joint venture with the University of Exeter, another Devonian institution, to establish the Peninsula College of Medicine and Dentistry. In 2011, this college was ranked 8th out of 30 UK universities for medicine. Its dental school, founded in 2006, provides free dental care to improve access to such services in the South West region.

input: While H2 is not very reactive under standard conditions, it does form compounds with most elements. Hydrogen can form compounds with elements that are more electronegative, such as halogens (e.g., F, Cl, Br, I), or oxygen; in these compounds hydrogen takes on a partial positive charge. When bonded to fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen, hydrogen can participate in a form of medium-strength noncovalent bonding with other similar molecules between their hydrogens called hydrogen bonding, which is critical to the stability of many biological molecules. Hydrogen also forms compounds with less electronegative elements, such as the metals and metalloids, in which it takes on a partial negative charge. These compounds are often known as hydrides.
rewrite: While hydrogen is not highly reactive under standard conditions, it does form compounds with most elements. It bonds with more electronegative elements, such as the halogens (e.g., F, Cl, Br, I) or oxygen, where hydrogen carries a partial positive charge. When attached to fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen, hydrogen can engage in a medium-strength noncovalent interaction known as hydrogen bonding, which is vital for the stability of many biological molecules. Conversely, hydrogen also forms compounds with less electronegative elements, including metals and metalloids, where it assumes a partial negative charge. These substances are commonly referred to as hydrides.

input: In 1877, Thomas Edison invented the phonograph. Unlike the phonautograph, it was capable of both recording and reproducing sound. Despite the similarity of name, there is no documentary evidence that Edison's phonograph was based on Scott's phonautograph. Edison first tried recording sound on a wax-impregnated paper tape, with the idea of creating a "telephone repeater" analogous to the telegraph repeater he had been working on. Although the visible results made him confident that sound could be physically recorded and reproduced, his notes do not indicate that he actually reproduced sound before his first experiment in which he used tinfoil as a recording medium several months later. The tinfoil was wrapped around a grooved metal cylinder and a sound-vibrated stylus indented the tinfoil while the cylinder was rotated. The recording could be played back immediately. The Scientific American article that introduced the tinfoil phonograph to the public mentioned Marey, Rosapelly and Barlow as well as Scott as creators of devices for recording but, importantly, not reproducing sound. Edison also invented variations of the phonograph that used tape and disc formats. Numerous applications for the phonograph were envisioned, but although it enjoyed a brief vogue as a startling novelty at public demonstrations, the tinfoil phonograph proved too crude to be put to any practical use. A decade later, Edison developed a greatly improved phonograph that used a hollow wax cylinder instead of a foil sheet. This proved to be both a better-sounding and far more useful and durable device. The wax phonograph cylinder created the recorded sound market at the end of the 1880s and dominated it through the early years of the 20th century.
rewrite: In 1877, Thomas Edison invented the phonograph, a device capable of both recording and reproducing sound, unlike the earlier phonautograph. There is no documentary evidence that Edison based his invention on Scott’s phonautograph, despite the similarity in their names. Edison initially experimented with recording sound on wax-impregnated paper tape, envisioning a "telephone repeater" similar to the telegraph repeater he had been developing. While the visible results from this test convinced him that sound could be physically recorded and reproduced, his notes do not show that he successfully reproduced sound until his first experiment using tinfoil several months later. In that experiment, tinfoil was wrapped around a grooved metal cylinder; a sound-vibrated stylus indented the foil as the cylinder rotated, and the recording could be played back immediately. An article in *Scientific American* that introduced the tinfoil phonograph to the public cited Marey, Rosapelly, Barlow, and Scott as inventors of devices that recorded—but did not reproduce—sound. Edison also created variations of the phonograph that employed tape and disc formats. Although many applications were imagined for the phonograph, and it briefly attracted attention as a novelty in public demonstrations, the tinfoil model was too crude for practical use. A decade later, Edison introduced a greatly improved phonograph that replaced the foil with a hollow wax cylinder. This new version produced better sound, was far more useful and durable, and created the recorded sound market at the end of the 1880s. The wax cylinder dominated that market through the early years of the 20th century.

input: San Diego County has one of the highest counts of animal and plant species that appear on the endangered species list among counties in the United States. Because of its diversity of habitat and its position on the Pacific Flyway, San Diego County has recorded the presence of 492 bird species, more than any other region in the country. San Diego always scores very high in the number of bird species observed in the annual Christmas Bird Count, sponsored by the Audubon Society, and it is known as one of the "birdiest" areas in the United States.
rewrite: San Diego County has one of the highest numbers of endangered animal and plant species among U.S. counties. Its diverse habitats and location on the Pacific Flyway support a remarkable 492 recorded bird species, more than any other region in the nation. The county consistently ranks very high in the annual Audubon Society Christmas Bird Count, reinforcing its reputation as one of the "birdiest" areas in the United States.

input: At the same time, these movements were influenced by, and in some respects continued, philosophical thought within the Vedic tradition as reflected e.g. in the Upanishads. These movements included, besides Buddhism, various skeptics (such as Sanjaya Belatthiputta), atomists (such as Pakudha Kaccayana), materialists (such as Ajita Kesakambali), antinomians (such as Purana Kassapa); the most important ones in the 5th century BCE were the Ajivikas, who emphasized the rule of fate, the Lokayata (materialists), the Ajnanas (agnostics) and the Jains, who stressed that the soul must be freed from matter. Many of these new movements shared the same conceptual vocabulary—atman ("Self"), buddha ("awakened one"), dhamma ("rule" or "law"), karma ("action"), nirvana ("extinguishing"), samsara ("eternal recurrence") and yoga ("spiritual practice").[note 24] The shramanas rejected the Veda, and the authority of the brahmans, who claimed they possessed revealed truths not knowable by any ordinary human means. Moreover, they declared that the entire Brahmanical system was fraudulent: a conspiracy of the brahmans to enrich themselves by charging exorbitant fees to perform bogus rites and give useless advice.
rewrite: Simultaneously, these movements were influenced by and, in certain ways, extended philosophical ideas from the Vedic tradition, such as those found in the Upanishads. Alongside Buddhism, they included various skeptics like Sanjaya Belatthiputta, atomists like Pakudha Kaccayana, materialists like Ajita Kesakambali, and antinomians like Purana Kassapa. The most significant groups in the 5th century BCE were the Ajivikas, who focused on the rule of fate; the Lokayata (materialists); the Ajnanas (agnostics); and the Jains, who emphasized freeing the soul from matter. Many of these new schools shared a common conceptual vocabulary—atman ("Self"), buddha ("awakened one"), dhamma ("rule" or "law"), karma ("action"), nirvana ("extinguishing"), samsara ("eternal recurrence"), and yoga ("spiritual practice"). The shramanas rejected the authority of the Vedas and the brahmans, who claimed to possess divinely revealed truths inaccessible to ordinary people. Furthermore, they denounced the entire Brahmanical system as a fraud: a brahmanical conspiracy to enrich themselves by charging excessive fees for performing false rites and offering useless advice.

input: In DC circuits and pulsed circuits, current and voltage reversal are affected by the damping of the system. Voltage reversal is encountered in RLC circuits that are under-damped. The current and voltage reverse direction, forming a harmonic oscillator between the inductance and capacitance. The current and voltage will tend to oscillate and may reverse direction several times, with each peak being lower than the previous, until the system reaches an equilibrium. This is often referred to as ringing. In comparison, critically damped or over-damped systems usually do not experience a voltage reversal. Reversal is also encountered in AC circuits, where the peak current will be equal in each direction.
rewrite: In DC and pulsed circuits, the damping of the system influences current and voltage reversal. Under-damped RLC circuits experience voltage reversal, where the current and voltage change direction, creating a harmonic oscillator between the inductance and capacitance. They tend to oscillate and may reverse direction multiple times, with each successive peak lower than the last, until equilibrium is reached—a phenomenon often called ringing. By contrast, critically damped or over-damped systems typically do not undergo voltage reversal. Reversal also occurs in AC circuits, where the peak current is equal in each direction.

input: In a June 2008 speech, President and CEO of the New York Federal Reserve Bank Timothy Geithner—who in 2009 became Secretary of the United States Treasury—placed significant blame for the freezing of credit markets on a "run" on the entities in the "parallel" banking system, also called the shadow banking system. These entities became critical to the credit markets underpinning the financial system, but were not subject to the same regulatory controls. Further, these entities were vulnerable because of maturity mismatch, meaning that they borrowed short-term in liquid markets to purchase long-term, illiquid and risky assets. This meant that disruptions in credit markets would make them subject to rapid deleveraging, selling their long-term assets at depressed prices. He described the significance of these entities:
rewrite: In a June 2008 speech, Timothy Geithner—then President and CEO of the New York Federal Reserve Bank and later the U.S. Treasury Secretary in 2009—largely attributed the credit market freeze to a "run" on the "parallel" or shadow banking system. These entities had become essential to the credit markets supporting the financial system, yet they operated outside the same regulatory controls. They were also vulnerable due to maturity mismatch, borrowing short-term in liquid markets to invest in long-term, illiquid, and risky assets. Consequently, any disruption in credit markets forced them into rapid deleveraging, selling their long-term assets at deeply discounted prices. Geithner underscored the critical role these entities played.

input: The AVL, created by the Valencian parliament, is in charge of dictating the official rules governing the use of Valencian, and its standard is based on the Norms of Castelló (Normes de Castelló). Currently, everyone who writes in Valencian uses this standard, except the Royal Academy of Valencian Culture (Acadèmia de Cultura Valenciana, RACV), which uses for Valencian an independent standard.
rewrite: The AVL, established by the Valencian parliament, dictates the official rules for Valencian usage, basing its standard on the Norms of Castelló. Today, all who write in Valencian follow this standard, except the Royal Academy of Valencian Culture (RACV), which employs an independent standard for the language.

input: Many instruments originated during the Renaissance; others were variations of, or improvements upon, instruments that had existed previously. Some have survived to the present day; others have disappeared, only to be recreated in order to perform music of the period on authentic instruments. As in the modern day, instruments may be classified as brass, strings, percussion, and woodwind.

Some of these instruments endure today, while others vanished only to be later recreated for historically accurate performances. Instruments from this period, much like modern ones, can be categorized as brass, strings, percussion, and woodwind.

input: Various classes of Vajrayana literature developed as a result of royal courts sponsoring both Buddhism and Saivism. The Mañjusrimulakalpa, which later came to classified under Kriyatantra, states that mantras taught in the Saiva, Garuda and Vaisnava tantras will be effective if applied by Buddhists since they were all taught originally by Manjushri. The Guhyasiddhi of Padmavajra, a work associated with the Guhyasamaja tradition, prescribes acting as a Saiva guru and initiating members into Saiva Siddhanta scriptures and mandalas. The Samvara tantra texts adopted the pitha list from the Saiva text Tantrasadbhava, introducing a copying error where a deity was mistaken for a place.
rewrite: Various classes of Vajrayana literature emerged as royal courts sponsored both Buddhism and Saivism. The Mañjusrimulakalpa, later classified as Kriyatantra, declares that mantras from Saiva, Garuda, and Vaisnava tantras are effective for Buddhists, as they were originally taught by Manjushri. The Guhyasiddhi of Padmavajra, a text from the Guhyasamaja tradition, instructs one to act as a Saiva guru and initiate followers into Saiva Siddhanta scriptures and mandalas. Additionally, the Samvara tantra texts borrowed their pitha list from the Saiva Tantrasadbhava, inadvertently copying an error where a deity's name was mistaken for a place.

input: The process was completed in 27 BC when the Roman Emperor Augustus annexed the rest of Greece and constituted it as the senatorial province of Achaea. Despite their military superiority, the Romans admired and became heavily influenced by the achievements of Greek culture, hence Horace's famous statement: Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit ("Greece, although captured, took its wild conqueror captive"). The epics of Homer inspired the Aeneid of Virgil, and authors such as Seneca the younger wrote using Greek styles. Roman heroes such as Scipio Africanus, tended to study philosophy and regarded Greek culture and science as an example to be followed. Similarly, most Roman emperors maintained an admiration for things Greek in nature. The Roman Emperor Nero visited Greece in AD 66, and performed at the Ancient Olympic Games, despite the rules against non-Greek participation. Hadrian was also particularly fond of the Greeks; before he became emperor he served as an eponymous archon of Athens.
rewrite: The process concluded in 27 BC when Emperor Augustus annexed the remaining Greek territories, organizing them into the senatorial province of Achaea. Despite their military dominance, the Romans greatly admired and were profoundly influenced by Greek cultural achievements. This is encapsulated in Horace’s famous line: *Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit* ("Captured Greece captured its wild conqueror"). Virgil’s *Aeneid* was inspired by Homer’s epics, and writers like Seneca the Younger adopted Greek literary styles. Roman heroes, such as Scipio Africanus, studied philosophy and viewed Greek culture and science as models to emulate. Most Roman emperors maintained a deep admiration for Greek culture. Emperor Nero visited Greece in AD 66 and performed at the Ancient Olympic Games, even though rules forbade non-Greek participation. Hadrian, particularly fond of the Greeks, had served as the eponymous archon of Athens before becoming emperor.

input: The managing director of London Weekend Television (LWT), Greg Dyke, met with the representatives of the "big five" football clubs in England in 1990. The meeting was to pave the way for a break away from The Football League. Dyke believed that it would be more lucrative for LWT if only the larger clubs in the country were featured on national television and wanted to establish whether the clubs would be interested in a larger share of television rights money. The five clubs decided it was a good idea and decided to press ahead with it; however, the league would have no credibility without the backing of The Football Association and so David Dein of Arsenal held talks to see whether the FA were receptive to the idea. The FA did not enjoy an amicable relationship with the Football League at the time and considered it as a way to weaken the Football League's position.
rewrite: In 1990, Greg Dyke, the managing director of London Weekend Television (LWT), met with representatives from England's "big five" football clubs. The purpose was to lay the groundwork for a breakaway from The Football League. Dyke believed that featuring only the country's larger clubs on national television would be more lucrative for LWT, and he sought to determine if the clubs were interested in securing a larger share of television rights revenue. The five clubs agreed it was a good idea and resolved to proceed. However, such a league would lack credibility without the support of The Football Association. Consequently, David Dein of Arsenal held talks to gauge the FA's receptiveness to the idea. At the time, the FA did not have an amicable relationship with the Football League and viewed the proposal as a potential means to weaken the League's position.

input: In abstract algebra, more general structures are defined by relaxing some of the axioms defining a group. For example, if the requirement that every element has an inverse is eliminated, the resulting algebraic structure is called a monoid. The natural numbers N (including 0) under addition form a monoid, as do the nonzero integers under multiplication (Z ∖ {0}, ·), see above. There is a general method to formally add inverses to elements to any (abelian) monoid, much the same way as (Q ∖ {0}, ·) is derived from (Z ∖ {0}, ·), known as the Grothendieck group. Groupoids are similar to groups except that the composition a • b need not be defined for all a and b. They arise in the study of more complicated forms of symmetry, often in topological and analytical structures, such as the fundamental groupoid or stacks. Finally, it is possible to generalize any of these concepts by replacing the binary operation with an arbitrary n-ary one (i.e. an operation taking n arguments). With the proper generalization of the group axioms this gives rise to an n-ary group. The table gives a list of several structures generalizing groups.
rewrite: In abstract algebra, more general structures are defined by relaxing certain group axioms. For instance, removing the requirement that every element has an inverse yields an algebraic structure called a monoid. The natural numbers N (including 0) under addition form a monoid, as do the nonzero integers under multiplication (Z ∖ {0}, ·), as noted earlier. There exists a general method to formally add inverses to the elements of any abelian monoid, similar to how (Q ∖ {0}, ·) is constructed from (Z ∖ {0}, ·); this is known as the Grothendieck group. Groupoids resemble groups, but their composition a • b is not necessarily defined for every pair a and b. They appear in the study of more complex forms of symmetry, frequently within topological and analytical contexts, such as in the fundamental groupoid or stacks. Lastly, these concepts can be further generalized by replacing the binary operation with an arbitrary n-ary operation (i.e., one taking n arguments). With a suitable adaptation of the group axioms, this leads to an n-ary group. The table provides a list of several structures that generalize groups.

input: The most notable cricket club in Cork is Cork County Cricket Club, which was formed in 1874. Although located within the Munster jurisdiction, the club plays in the Leinster Senior League. The club plays at the Mardyke, a ground which has hosted three first-class matches in 1947, 1961 and 1973. All three involved Ireland playing Scotland. The Cork Cricket Academy operates within the city, with the stated aim of introducing the sport to schools in the city and county. Cork's other main cricket club, Harlequins Cricket Club, play close to Cork Airport.
rewrite: The most notable cricket club in Cork is Cork County Cricket Club, founded in 1874. Despite being within the Munster jurisdiction, the club competes in the Leinster Senior League. Its home ground is the Mardyke, which hosted three first-class matches in 1947, 1961, and 1973; all three were between Ireland and Scotland. Also within the city is the Cork Cricket Academy, aimed at introducing the sport to local schools. The other main club, Harlequins Cricket Club, is located near Cork Airport.

input: Throughout its prehistory and early history, the region and its vicinity in the Yangtze region was the cradle of unique local civilizations which can be dated back to at least the 15th century BC and coinciding with the later years of the Shang and Zhou dynasties in North China. Sichuan was referred to in ancient Chinese sources as Ba-Shu (巴蜀), an abbreviation of the kingdoms of Ba and Shu which existed within the Sichuan Basin. Ba included Chongqing and the land in eastern Sichuan along the Yangtze and some tributary streams, while Shu included today's Chengdu, its surrounding plain and adjacent territories in western Sichuan.
rewrite: Throughout its prehistory and early history, the Yangtze region was the cradle of unique local civilizations. These can be traced back to at least the 15th century BC, a period coinciding with the later years of the Shang and Zhou dynasties in North China. Ancient Chinese sources referred to Sichuan as Ba-Shu (巴蜀), an abbreviation for the kingdoms of Ba and Shu within the Sichuan Basin. The kingdom of Ba encompassed Chongqing and eastern Sichuan along the Yangtze and its tributaries. Shu included present-day Chengdu, its surrounding plain, and adjacent territories in western Sichuan.

input: In addressing the question of who invented the incandescent lamp, historians Robert Friedel and Paul Israel list 22 inventors of incandescent lamps prior to Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison. They conclude that Edison's version was able to outstrip the others because of a combination of three factors: an effective incandescent material, a higher vacuum than others were able to achieve (by use of the Sprengel pump) and a high resistance that made power distribution from a centralized source economically viable.
rewrite: When considering who invented the incandescent lamp, historians Robert Friedel and Paul Israel name 22 inventors who preceded Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison. They argue Edison’s lamp surpassed the others due to three key factors: an efficient incandescent material, a higher vacuum achieved with the Sprengel pump, and a high resistance that allowed cost-effective centralized power distribution.

input: Literature consists of written productions, often restricted to those deemed to have artistic or intellectual value. Its Latin root literatura/litteratura (derived itself from littera, letter or handwriting) was used to refer to all written accounts, but intertwined with the roman concept of cultura: learning or cultivation. Literature often uses language differently than ordinary language (see literariness). Literature can be classified according to whether it is fiction or non-fiction and whether it is poetry or prose; it can be further distinguished according to major forms such as the novel, short story or drama; and works are often categorised according to historical periods or their adherence to certain aesthetic features or expectations (genre).
rewrite: Literature encompasses written works, typically those considered to possess artistic or intellectual merit. The term originates from the Latin *literatura/litteratura* (derived from *littera*, meaning letter or handwriting), which referred to all written accounts and was connected to the Roman concept of *cultura*, or cultivation. Literature frequently employs language in ways distinct from ordinary usage (referred to as literariness). It can be classified as fiction or non-fiction and as poetry or prose. Further distinctions include major forms like the novel, short story, or drama. Works are also often categorized by historical period or their alignment with specific aesthetic features and expectations (genre).

input: The court ruled in 2014, after lengthy testimony, that at least two districts had to be redrawn because of gerrymandering. After this was appealed, in July 2015 the Florida Supreme Court ruled that lawmakers had followed an illegal and unconstitutional process overly influenced by party operatives, and ruled that at least eight districts had to be redrawn. On December 2, 2015, a 5-2 majority of the Court accepted a new map of congressional districts, some of which was drawn by challengers. Their ruling affirmed the map previously approved by Leon County Judge Terry Lewis, who had overseen the original trial. It particularly makes changes in South Florida. There are likely to be additional challenges to the map and districts.
rewrite: In 2014, the court ruled that at least two districts required redrawing due to gerrymandering. Following an appeal, the Florida Supreme Court decided in July 2015 that lawmakers had used an illegal and unconstitutional process unduly shaped by party operatives, ordering at least eight districts to be redrawn. On December 2, 2015, the Court, by a 5-2 majority, accepted a new congressional map—partially drawn by challengers—which affirmed the map earlier approved by Leon County Judge Terry Lewis, the overseer of the original trial. The changes particularly affect South Florida. Further challenges to the map and districts are likely.

input: All signatories to the CPPCG are required to prevent and punish acts of genocide, both in peace and wartime, though some barriers make this enforcement difficult. In particular, some of the signatories—namely, Bahrain, Bangladesh, India, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, the United States, Vietnam, Yemen, and former Yugoslavia—signed with the proviso that no claim of genocide could be brought against them at the International Court of Justice without their consent. Despite official protests from other signatories (notably Cyprus and Norway) on the ethics and legal standing of these reservations, the immunity from prosecution they grant has been invoked from time to time, as when the United States refused to allow a charge of genocide brought against it by former Yugoslavia following the 1999 Kosovo War.
rewrite: All signatories to the CPPCG are obligated to prevent and punish genocide during both peace and war, yet enforcement faces significant barriers. Notably, several signatories—including Bahrain, Bangladesh, India, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, the United States, Vietnam, Yemen, and the former Yugoslavia—ratified the convention with a specific reservation. This proviso stipulates that no genocide claim can be brought against them at the International Court of Justice without their explicit consent. Although other signatories, such as Cyprus and Norway, have formally protested the ethics and legality of these reservations, the conferred immunity has been invoked in practice. For example, the United States invoked this reservation to reject a genocide charge filed against it by the former Yugoslavia after the 1999 Kosovo War.

input: In the high villages people live in homes built according to medieval designs that withstand cold winters. The kitchen is separated from the living area (called the stube, the area of the home heated by a stove), and second-floor bedrooms benefit from rising heat. The typical Swiss chalet originated in the Bernese Oberland. Chalets often face south or downhill, and are built of solid wood, with a steeply gabled roof to allow accumulated snow to slide off easily. Stairs leading to upper levels are sometimes built on the outside, and balconies are sometimes enclosed.
rewrite: In the high villages, homes are constructed using medieval designs to endure cold winters. The kitchen is separate from the living area, known as the stube, which is heated by a stove. Bedrooms on the second floor benefit from this rising heat. The classic Swiss chalet originated in the Bernese Oberland. These chalets, often facing south or downhill, are built from solid wood with steeply gabled roofs that allow snow to slide off easily. Outside stairs sometimes lead to upper levels, and balconies are occasionally enclosed.

input: Like other governmental economic activities, also privatization, such as in the sale of government-owned property, is particularly at the risk of cronyism. Privatizations in Russia, Latin America, and East Germany were accompanied by large-scale corruption during the sale of the state owned companies. Those with political connections unfairly gained large wealth, which has discredited privatization in these regions. While media have reported widely the grand corruption that accompanied the sales, studies have argued that in addition to increased operating efficiency, daily petty corruption is, or would be, larger without privatization, and that corruption is more prevalent in non-privatized sectors. Furthermore, there is evidence to suggest that extralegal and unofficial activities are more prevalent in countries that privatized less.
rewrite: Like other government economic activities, privatization—such as the sale of state-owned assets—is especially vulnerable to cronyism. In Russia, Latin America, and East Germany, privatizations were marked by extensive corruption during the sale of state-owned companies. Politically connected individuals unfairly amassed considerable wealth, which has tarnished the reputation of privatization in these areas. Although the media have widely covered the grand corruption linked to these sales, studies contend that, aside from boosting operational efficiency, daily petty corruption is or would be greater without privatization, and that corruption is more widespread in non-privatized sectors. Moreover, evidence suggests extralegal and unofficial activities are more common in countries that privatized less.

input: Marvel held its own comic book convention, Marvelcon '75, in spring 1975, and promised a Marvelcon '76. At the 1975 event, Stan Lee used a Fantastic Four panel discussion to announce that Jack Kirby, the artist co-creator of most of Marvel's signature characters, was returning to Marvel after having left in 1970 to work for rival DC Comics. In October 1976, Marvel, which already licensed reprints in different countries, including the UK, created a superhero specifically for the British market. Captain Britain debuted exclusively in the UK, and later appeared in American comics.

Kirby had left Marvel in 1970 to work for rival DC Comics. Then, in October 1976, Marvel, which already licensed reprints internationally including in the UK, created a superhero specifically for the British market.
